blocks.text: This chapter explores applications of computer science through emerging technologies: artificial intelligence (AI) in voice assistants, chatbots and image recognition, with its benefits and challenges; the Internet of Things (IoT), where connected devices collect and share data for automation; the cultural and ethical implications of AI, including fairness, transparency and the roles of stakeholders; how these technologies can address Pakistan's national challenges, such as through smart agriculture; and the policies, regulations and responsible innovation needed for ethical, sustainable use.

Emerging technologies are advanced innovations that are changing how people live, work and communicate. AI, the Internet of Things, cloud computing and blockchain are reshaping industries and creating smarter systems for managing data, automation and connectivity (Fig 8.1). They drive innovation in healthcare, education, transport and agriculture, but also raise issues such as data security, ethics and dependence on automation; understanding them helps people use them responsibly.

blocks.alt: A central circle labelled smarter systems is joined to four boxes: Artificial Intelligence (learns from data; decides), Internet of Things (devices sense and act), Cloud Computing (storage and computing online) and Blockchain (shared, tamper-proof records). A note says they are used across healthcare, education, transport and agriculture and also raise security and ethical questions.
blocks.caption: AI, IoT, cloud computing and blockchain working together (original diagram after Fig 8.1).
blocks.long_description: The four often combine: IoT devices collect data, the cloud stores it, AI learns from it and blockchain keeps a trusted record.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Emerging technologies such as AI, IoT, cloud computing and blockchain are shaping the next digital revolution, connecting people, data and devices across the world.

AI is the branch of computer science that enables machines to do tasks that normally need human intelligence (Fig 8.2). AI systems analyse data, recognise patterns and make decisions with little human input. They learn through machine learning: algorithms are trained on large datasets to find trends, and the more data they process, the more accurate they become. AI combines data, algorithms and computing power to understand speech, detect objects in images and predict outcomes, using techniques such as neural networks and natural language processing (NLP) that are inspired by how the brain processes information.

items: Voice assistants (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant) understand spoken commands and respond.
Chatbots on websites answer customers' questions, such as 'Where is my order?', for thousands of users at once (Amazon, Daraz).
Image recognition identifies faces, objects or medical conditions in photos and scans.
Recommendation systems (YouTube, Daraz, Amazon) suggest videos or products from user preferences.
Self-driving cars interpret their surroundings to make driving decisions.

blocks.caption: Benefits and challenges of AI
rows: Repetitive tasks done faster than people
Helping doctors diagnose disease, e.g. DeepMind's AI predicting eye diseases such as glaucoma from 3D eye scans
Bias in algorithms leading to unfair outcomes
Businesses analysing customer behaviour and predicting trends; personalised learning and adaptive tutoring
Decisions that affect people's lives raise ethical questions

blocks.text: Balancing innovation with responsibility keeps AI a tool that benefits people rather than harms them.

blocks.alt: Data, algorithms and computing power feed into an AI model (machine learning), which produces vision (images, faces), speech and language (NLP), and decisions and predictions. Below, a green benefits box lists faster repetitive work, diagnosis support, chatbots, personalised learning and crop monitoring, and a red challenges box lists data privacy, job displacement, bias and decisions that affect people's lives.
blocks.caption: How AI works, with its benefits and challenges (original diagram after Fig 8.2).
blocks.long_description: The same model that helps a doctor can also make an unfair decision if its training data is biased, which is why benefits and challenges come together.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Farmers use AI with drones and sensors to monitor crops, helping them increase yield and reduce waste.

The Internet of Things is a network of physical devices connected through the Internet that can collect, share and act on data. The devices contain sensors, processors and communication hardware; they link by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or mobile networks and exchange data with each other or a central platform. Everyday objects such as lights, thermostats and appliances can then be monitored and controlled remotely, creating smart environments that work with little human effort.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: IoT connects everyday devices such as fridges, cars and lights so they can 'talk' to each other automatically.

items: Smart homes: lighting, heating, curtains and security controlled by phone apps or voice. Smart LED bulbs can switch on at 6:00 p.m.; curtains can open with the morning alarm and close when the room goes above 35 C; thermostats follow user preferences; cameras send alerts to phones. This adds comfort, saves energy and improves safety (Fig 8.3).
Healthcare: sensors monitor heart rate, blood pressure and glucose in real time, so doctors can track patients remotely and respond quickly in emergencies.
Agriculture: devices measure soil moisture, temperature and weather to plan irrigation and crop management, raising yields and reducing waste.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Smart homes, wearable fitness bands and smart farms are all powered by IoT technology.

IoT works through three functions. Data collection: sensors measure the environment, such as temperature, movement or humidity. Communication: the data is sent to cloud systems or servers to be processed and analysed, keeping devices synchronised. Automation: the analysed data triggers actions, such as switching off lights in an empty room or starting irrigation when the soil is dry, which saves time and reduces human error.

blocks.alt: On the left three input sensors (temperature, motion and light) feed a controller, a microcontroller such as an ESP32. The controller exchanges data with the Internet or cloud, which connects to a mobile app and to three output actuators on the right: smart light, smart fan and smart socket. A note gives example rules: lights on at 6:00 p.m., curtains close above 35 C, cameras send alerts to the phone.
blocks.caption: A smart home built with IoT (original diagram after Fig 8.3).
blocks.long_description: Sensors sense, the controller and cloud decide, and actuators act; the phone app lets the user watch and override the system.

Cloud computing lets users store, manage and process data on remote servers on the Internet instead of on their own computers (Fig 8.4). The servers are managed by cloud service providers, so data and applications can be reached anytime, anywhere, with an Internet connection, and most processing happens remotely. Individuals and businesses use online storage, web hosting and software without maintaining hardware; streaming, online learning and shared workspaces all depend on it.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Saving a document on Google Drive or iCloud is using cloud computing.

items: Scalability: storage and computing power can be increased or reduced as needed, which suits growing organisations.
Accessibility: work from many devices and places without copying files by hand.
Cost-effectiveness: no need for expensive servers and maintenance staff; users pay only for what they use (pay-as-you-go).
Examples: Amazon Web Services (AWS) for hosting, storage and app development; Microsoft Azure for building and managing applications in the cloud.

blocks.alt: Clients (laptop, phone, tablet, desktop) reach four layers through the Internet. Service models: SaaS (ready software such as Gmail and Office 365), PaaS (build apps, e.g. Google App Engine) and IaaS (raw computing such as virtual machines). Management: billing, monitoring and scaling, security. Deployment: public, private and hybrid cloud. Infrastructure: servers and storage, databases and networking, data centres.
blocks.caption: Cloud computing in layers (original diagram after Fig 8.4).
blocks.long_description: Google Drive is a SaaS product people use directly; AWS and Azure are platforms that offer all three service models to businesses and developers.

blocks.text: Blockchain is a digital system that stores and shares information across many computers instead of one central server. Each verified record, or block, links to the one before it, forming a chain that cannot easily be changed; because every computer holds a copy, altering data without detection is nearly impossible. This decentralised design increases transparency, security and trust, removing the need for intermediaries such as banks and allowing direct, accountable exchanges.

items: Finance: cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin for secure peer-to-peer transactions.
Supply chains: tracking goods from origin to customer to prove they are genuine.
Data security: tamper-proof storage of legal documents, medical files and certificates.
Governments, companies and schools: land records, supply chains and academic credentials.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: From cryptocurrency to supply-chain tracking, blockchain builds trust through transparency.
